newsitem.title: ITALY: OPINION - Italian industry and the Euro - by By Innocenzo Cipolletta.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Italian industry and the Euro - by By Innocenzo Cipolletta.

text.p: By Innocenzo Cipolletta, Director General, Italian employers' fedderation.

ROME - The participation of the Italian economy in the third and last phase of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the adoption of a single currency are major objectives for Italian industrialists.
That is why the Italian business community is looking forward to Italy participating in European Monetary Union from the outset.
At the same time, Italian industrialists think that it is important to stick to criteria and time schedules as established in the Maastricht Treaty.
The motives behind the deep interest of Italian industrialists in the single currency are both economic and political. Economic motivations are mainly threefold:
-- Microeconomic benefits coming from stability, elimination of the exchange risk and transaction costs connected to the use of multiple currencies in international trade and investment;

-- The single currency will reinforce integration among member countries, making European Monetary Union a single, highly integrated economic system; Italy cannot run the risk of remaining excluded from this area which represents the most important market for Italian products and investment; about 60 percent of Italian trade is with European countries; more than 50 percent of outward and inward Italian foreign direct investment is with European Union countries.

-- The adoption of the single currency would imply the immediate reduction of Italian interest rates to the level prevailing in Europe with highly positive repercussions for Italian public finance, private fixed capital formation, economic growth and employment.
Besides these economic reasons, there is a more general political motivation behind industrialists' support for the project: the single currency is an essential step toward European political union.

It is in the interest of Italian entrepreneurs to be part of a large and powerful political area, with strong leadership and with the capacity to have a common foreign policy and to deal, as a unique political entity, with other large political systems on an equal footing.

For all these reasons Italian industrialists are pressing for an acceleration of convergence towards the criteria set out in the Maastricht treaty. In the last four years Italy has made a substantial step forward in the direction of fiscal adjustment and reduction of inflation. The distance to cover in order to complete the convergence process is not small, but we have the possibility to succeed in this effort.

In particular, there are two main preconditions for completing the convergence process -- the confirmation and relaunch of an incomes policy along the lines of the agreement of July 1993 and an acceleration of fiscal adjustment.

As far as the latter is concerned, the Italian budget law for 1997 is large and important. However it does not ensure convergence towards the "Maastricht-target" for the public sector deficit. Italian industrialists think the Government should adopt next year a supplementary budget as soon as it becomes apparent that the public sector deficit is out of line.

Moreover, it will be necessary to prepare in due course all the necessary cuts of those public expenditure items (pension, health spending and public sector wages) that have not been touched in the 1997 budget plan. These cuts will be necessary to ensure that the reduction of the public sector deficit is permanent and not just the result of so called "una-tantum' (one off) measures.

Finally, these cuts are important to complete the reform of the Italian welfare system and to allow in the medium and long run a reduction of the tax burden that has reached in the last few years extremely high levels in the Italian economy.
(The opinions expressed in this column represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters).
